title: Jungfrau Maleen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 198. Text from Wikisource („Jungfrau Maleen (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale's prose is in High German; its nine sung or spoken verse passages are in Low German (Plattdeutsch), with the High German equivalent given alongside in the glossary.
about: “Jungfrau Maleen,” KHM 198, walls its heroine into a lightless tower for seven years because she will not take the husband her father chose, and then forgets her there; a bread knife and three days’ work at the mortar get her out, into a kingdom burnt to the ground. She surfaces as a kitchen drudge at the court of the man she had been promised to, and is forced on pain of death to put on the ugly bride’s clothes and walk to the church in her place — speaking as she goes to a nettle bush, a churchyard footbridge and the church door. Those three sayings, her repetition of them when the false bride comes to demand what was said, the bride’s own rhyme for getting out of the bedchamber, and the song children sang afterwards at the foot of the tower are the nine Low German passages in an otherwise High German tale, with the High German alongside in the glossary; the beheading that closes it gets one line and no comment.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein König, der hatte einen Sohn, der warb um die Tochter eines mächtigen Königs, die hieß Jungfrau Maleen und war wunderschön.
sentences.l: There was once a king, he had a son, who wooed the daughter of a mighty king; she was called Maiden Maleen and was wondrously beautiful.
sentences.i: There was once a king who had a son, and the son wooed the daughter of a mighty king; she was called Maiden Maleen, and she was wondrously beautiful.
sentences.n: “der hatte einen Sohn” is the storyteller’s loose relative — ‘there was a king, he had a son’ — rather than a tight subordinate clause. “warb um” is werben um, to sue for a woman’s hand. “Jungfrau” here is simply ‘maiden’, an unmarried girl of rank. The prose of this tale is ordinary 1857 High German, but every song in it, and one spoken formula, switches into Low German; the first comes a few sentences on.

sentences.t: Weil ihr Vater sie einem andern geben wollte, so ward sie ihm versagt.
sentences.l: Because her father wanted to give her to another, she was refused him.
sentences.i: Because her father meant to give her to another, she was denied him.
sentences.n: “ward” is the older form of wurde (was, became), and it runs all through this tale. “versagen” here means to refuse or deny somebody something, not the modern ‘to fail’. The “so” heading the main clause simply answers the “weil”; German often marks the return like that, and English drops it.

sentences.t: Da sich aber beide von Herzen liebten, so wollten sie nicht von einander lassen, und die Jungfrau Maleen sprach zu ihrem Vater „ich kann und will keinen andern zu meinem Gemahl nehmen.“
sentences.l: But since the two loved each other from the heart, they would not let go of one another, and Maiden Maleen said to her father “I cannot and will not take any other for my husband.”
sentences.i: But since the two loved each other dearly, they would not give one another up, and Maiden Maleen said to her father, “I cannot and will not take any other man for my husband.”
sentences.n: “von Herzen” = from the heart, dearly. “von einander lassen” is to leave off one another, to part. “Gemahl” is the elevated word for a husband; the plain word would be Mann.

sentences.t: Da gerieth der Vater in Zorn und ließ einen finstern Thurn bauen, in den kein Strahl von Sonne oder Mond fiel.
sentences.l: Then the father fell into a rage and had a dark tower built, into which no ray of sun or moon fell.
sentences.i: Then the father flew into a rage and had a dark tower built, into which no ray of sun or moon fell.
sentences.n: “gerieth” is the 1857 spelling of geriet — in Zorn geraten, to fly into a rage. The th of Thurn, Thür and thun is everywhere in this printing and went out with the spelling reform of 1901. “ließ … bauen” = had it built.

sentences.t: Als er fertig war, sprach er „darin sollst du sieben Jahre lang sitzen, dann will ich kommen und sehen ob dein trotziger Sinn gebrochen ist.“
sentences.l: When it was finished, he said “in there you shall sit seven years long, then I will come and see whether your defiant spirit is broken.”
sentences.i: When it was finished, he said, “In there you shall sit for seven years, and then I will come and see whether your defiant spirit is broken.”
sentences.n: “sitzen” here carries its old sense of being imprisoned. “ob” introduces the indirect question and pushes its verb to the end. “trotzig” = defiant, stubborn.

sentences.t: Für die sieben Jahre ward Speise und Trank in den Thurn getragen, dann ward sie und ihre Kammerjungfer hinein geführt und eingemauert, und also von Himmel und Erde geschieden.
sentences.l: For the seven years food and drink were carried into the tower, then she and her chambermaid were led inside and walled in, and thus parted from heaven and earth.
sentences.i: Food and drink for the seven years were carried into the tower; then she and her waiting-maid were led inside and walled in, and so cut off from heaven and earth.
sentences.n: Twice “ward” builds a passive — was carried, was led. “also” here is the old ‘thus, in this way’, and is not the English ‘also’. “eingemauert” is the flat word for it: bricked in. The tale states the cruelty plainly and offers no comment on it.

sentences.t: Da saßen sie in der Finsternis, wußten nicht wann Tag oder Nacht anbrach.
sentences.l: There they sat in the darkness, did not know when day or night broke.
sentences.i: There they sat in the darkness, and did not know when day broke or night fell.
sentences.n: The subject is dropped in the second clause — ‘sat … did not know’ — which German allows when it does not change. “anbrechen” is the verb used of day and night beginning. The printing has Finsternis here and Finsterniß later; both are left as they stand.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn gieng oft um den Thurn herum und rief ihren Namen, aber kein Laut drang von außen durch die dicken Mauern.
sentences.l: The king’s son often went round about the tower and called her name, but no sound pressed through the thick walls from outside.
sentences.i: The king’s son often walked round the tower and called her name, but no sound came through the thick walls from outside.
sentences.n: “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging. “um … herum” wraps around its noun. “Laut” here is the noun der Laut, a sound, and not the adverb ‘loud’ the same spelling is elsewhere. “drang” is from dringen, to press or force its way through.

sentences.t: Was konnten sie anders thun als jammern und klagen?
sentences.l: What could they do other than wail and lament?
sentences.i: What could they do but wail and lament?
sentences.n: “thun” = tun in the 1857 spelling. After “anders”, the “als” means ‘than, but’.

sentences.t: Indessen gieng die Zeit dahin und an der Abnahme von Speise und Trank merkten sie daß die sieben Jahre ihrem Ende sich näherten.
sentences.l: Meanwhile the time went by, and by the dwindling of food and drink they noticed that the seven years were drawing towards their end.
sentences.i: Meanwhile time went by, and by the dwindling of the food and drink they knew that the seven years were drawing to a close.
sentences.n: “Abnahme” is the noun of abnehmen, to grow less — the stores going down are their only calendar. “dahingehen” is used of time passing away. In the daß-clause the reflexive slides in before the verb at the end: ihrem Ende sich näherten.

sentences.t: Sie dachten der Augenblick ihrer Erlösung wäre gekommen, aber kein Hammerschlag ließ sich hören und kein Stein wollte aus der Mauer fallen: es schien als ob ihr Vater sie vergessen hätte.
sentences.l: They thought the moment of their deliverance had come, but no hammer-blow let itself be heard and no stone would fall out of the wall: it seemed as though their father had forgotten them.
sentences.i: They thought the hour of their deliverance had come, but not a hammer-blow was to be heard and not a stone would fall out of the wall: it seemed their father had forgotten them.
sentences.n: “wäre” and “hätte” are the subjunctive of reported thought — this is what the two believed, not what the tale asserts. “ließ sich hören” = made itself heard. “Erlösung” is release, deliverance, and carries a faint religious weight.

sentences.t: Als sie nur noch für kurze Zeit Nahrung hatten und einen jämmerlichen Tod voraus sahen, da sprach die Jungfrau Maleen „wir müssen das letzte versuchen und sehen ob wir die Mauer durchbrechen.“
sentences.l: When they had food for only a short time yet and saw a wretched death before them, then Maiden Maleen said “we must try the last thing and see whether we break through the wall.”
sentences.i: When their food would last only a little longer and they saw a wretched death ahead of them, Maiden Maleen said, “We must try the last thing there is, and see whether we can break through the wall.”
sentences.n: “voraus sehen” = to see ahead, foresee, with its particle split off. “das letzte versuchen” is the fixed turn for trying the last resort. There is no ‘can’ in “ob wir die Mauer durchbrechen”; the plain present carries it.

sentences.t: Sie nahm das Brotmesser, grub und bohrte an dem Mörtel eines Steins, und wenn sie müd war, so löste sie die Kammerjungfer ab.
sentences.l: She took the bread-knife, dug and bored at the mortar of a stone, and when she was tired, the chambermaid relieved her.
sentences.i: She took the bread knife and dug and bored at the mortar round a stone, and when she was tired the waiting-maid took over from her.
sentences.n: The bread knife is the only tool they have, and the tale hands it over without ceremony. “ablösen” = to relieve somebody at a task, separable: löste … ab. “müd” is the older short form of müde.

sentences.t: Nach langer Arbeit gelang es ihnen einen Stein heraus zu nehmen, dann einen zweiten und dritten,
sentences.l: After long labour it succeeded for them to take out one stone, then a second and a third,
sentences.i: After long labour they managed to get one stone out, then a second and a third,
sentences.n: “es gelang ihnen” is impersonal — literally ‘it succeeded to them’ — where English says ‘they managed’. The printing writes heraus zu nehmen in three words where modern spelling glues them together.

sentences.t: und nach drei Tagen fiel der erste Lichtstrahl in ihre Dunkelheit, und endlich war die Öffnung so groß daß sie hinaus schauen konnten.
sentences.l: and after three days the first ray of light fell into their darkness, and at last the opening was so large that they could look out.
sentences.i: and after three days the first ray of light fell into their darkness, and at last the opening was large enough for them to look out.
sentences.n: “Lichtstrahl” is Licht plus Strahl, a ray of light; German builds such compounds freely. “hinaus schauen”, again printed apart, is hinausschauen.

sentences.t: Der Himmel war blau, und eine frische Luft wehte ihnen entgegen, aber wie traurig sah rings umher alles aus:
sentences.l: The sky was blue, and a fresh air blew towards them, but how sorrowful everything round about looked:
sentences.i: The sky was blue and a fresh wind blew in upon them, but how mournful everything looked round about:
sentences.n: “entgegen wehen” = to blow towards; “rings umher” = all around. “aussehen” is split, its particle waiting at the end: sah … aus.

sentences.t: das Schloß ihres Vaters lag in Trümmern, die Stadt und die Dörfer waren, so weit man sehen konnte, verbrannt,
sentences.l: her father’s castle lay in ruins, the town and the villages were, as far as one could see, burnt,
sentences.i: her father’s castle lay in ruins, the town and the villages burnt as far as one could see,
sentences.n: The colon before this is doing the work of ‘namely’. The interjected “so weit man sehen konnte” sits between the auxiliary and its participle, which German allows and English cannot.

sentences.t: die Felder weit und breit verheert: keine Menschenseele ließ sich erblicken.
sentences.l: the fields far and wide laid waste: not a human soul let itself be seen.
sentences.i: the fields laid waste far and wide: not a living soul was to be seen.
sentences.n: The verb is left out — ‘the fields [were] laid waste’ — the gapping German does easily after a parallel clause. “ließ sich erblicken” is the same turn as ließ sich hören above.

sentences.t: Als die Öffnung in der Mauer so groß war, daß sie hindurchschlüpfen konnten, so sprang zuerst die Kammerjungfer herab und dann folgte die Jungfrau Maleen.
sentences.l: When the opening in the wall was so large that they could slip through it, the chambermaid sprang down first and then Maiden Maleen followed.
sentences.i: When the opening in the wall was large enough for them to slip through, the waiting-maid jumped down first and Maiden Maleen followed.
sentences.n: “hindurchschlüpfen” = to slip through. How far down the drop was, the tale does not say.

sentences.t: Aber wo sollten sie sich hinwenden?
sentences.l: But where were they to turn themselves?
sentences.i: But where were they to turn?
sentences.n: “sich hinwenden” = to turn oneself somewhere. “sollten” here is not ‘should’ in the moral sense but ‘were to’.

sentences.t: Die Feinde hatten das ganze Reich verwüstet, den König verjagt und alle Einwohner erschlagen.
sentences.l: The enemies had laid waste the whole kingdom, driven out the king and slain all the inhabitants.
sentences.i: The enemy had laid the whole kingdom waste, driven out the king and slain all the inhabitants.
sentences.n: Three past participles hang on the single hatten at the front — verwüstet, verjagt, erschlagen — a chain German builds without repeating the auxiliary. The seven years in the dark have cost her the world outside as well.

sentences.t: Sie wanderten fort um ein anderes Land zu suchen, aber sie fanden nirgend ein Obdach oder einen Menschen, der ihnen einen Bissen Brot gab,
sentences.l: They wandered on to seek another land, but they found nowhere a shelter or a person who gave them a bite of bread,
sentences.i: They wandered on to look for another country, but nowhere did they find a roof or a soul to give them a bite of bread,
sentences.n: “fortwandern” splits: wanderten … fort. “nirgend” is the older form of nirgends. “um … zu suchen” is the ordinary purpose clause.

sentences.t: und ihre Noth war so groß daß sie ihren Hunger an einem Brennesselstrauch stillen mußten.
sentences.l: and their need was so great that they had to still their hunger at a nettle bush.
sentences.i: and their need was so great that they had to stay their hunger on a nettle bush.
sentences.n: “Noth” = Not in the 1857 spelling. The nettle bush is planted here for the song that comes later: the false bride will be caught out by a line about eating nettles raw.

sentences.t: Als sie nach langer Wanderung in ein anderes Land kamen, boten sie überall ihre Dienste an, aber wo sie anklopften wurden sie abgewiesen, und niemand wollte sich ihrer erbarmen.
sentences.l: When after long wandering they came into another land, they offered their services everywhere, but where they knocked they were rejected, and nobody wanted to take pity on them.
sentences.i: When after long wandering they came into another country, they offered their services everywhere, but wherever they knocked they were turned away, and nobody would take pity on them.
sentences.n: “anbieten” splits — boten … an. “sich jemandes erbarmen” takes the genitive: ihrer, ‘of them’, an old construction modern German has mostly given up.

sentences.t: Endlich gelangten sie in eine große Stadt und giengen nach dem königlichen Hof.
sentences.l: At last they reached a great city and went to the royal court.
sentences.i: At last they came to a great city and went to the royal court.
sentences.n: “gelangen” = to reach, arrive at, a shade more formal than kommen. “Hof” is both the court and the courtyard; here it is the court, and later in the tale it is the yard.

sentences.t: Aber auch da hieß man sie weiter gehen, bis endlich der Koch sagte sie könnten in der Küche bleiben und als Aschenputtel dienen.
sentences.l: But there too they were bidden go further on, until at last the cook said they could stay in the kitchen and serve as ash-girls.
sentences.i: But there too they were told to move on, until at last the cook said they might stay in the kitchen and serve as scullery-maids.
sentences.n: “hieß man sie” — the impersonal man with heißen in its old sense, to bid somebody do something. “der Koch” here is the noun, the cook, and not the imperative of kochen. “Aschenputtel” is the ash-grubber, the kitchen drudge — the name of the Cinderella tale used here as a common noun. “könnten” is the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: Der Sohn des Königs, in dessen Reich sie sich befanden, war aber gerade der Verlobte der Jungfrau Maleen gewesen.
sentences.l: But the son of the king in whose kingdom they found themselves had been precisely the betrothed of Maiden Maleen.
sentences.i: Now the son of the king in whose kingdom they had landed was the very man who had been betrothed to Maiden Maleen.
sentences.n: “gerade” here means ‘precisely, none other than’. “sich befinden” = to find oneself, to be somewhere. The whole plot turns on this sentence, and the tale drops it in without ceremony.

sentences.t: Der Vater hatte ihm eine andere Braut bestimmt, die ebenso häßlich von Angesicht als bös von Herzen war.
sentences.l: The father had appointed him another bride, who was as ugly of face as she was wicked of heart.
sentences.i: His father had chosen another bride for him, one as ugly in face as she was wicked in heart.
sentences.n: “ebenso … als” is the older comparison where modern German says ebenso … wie. “von Angesicht”, “von Herzen” — in respect of face, in respect of heart. “Braut” covers both the betrothed and the bride.

sentences.t: Die Hochzeit war festgesetzt und die Braut schon angelangt, bei ihrer großen Häßlichkeit aber ließ sie sich vor niemand sehen und schloß sich in ihre Kammer ein,
sentences.l: The wedding was appointed and the bride already arrived; but given her great ugliness she let herself be seen before nobody and shut herself into her chamber,
sentences.i: The wedding was fixed and the bride already arrived; but because she was so ugly she let no one set eyes on her and shut herself up in her chamber,
sentences.n: “bei ihrer großen Häßlichkeit” — bei here means ‘given, in view of’. “sich sehen lassen” = to show oneself. “sich einschließen” splits: schloß sich … ein.

sentences.t: und die Jungfrau Maleen mußte ihr das Essen aus der Küche bringen.
sentences.l: and Maiden Maleen had to bring her the food from the kitchen.
sentences.i: and Maiden Maleen had to carry her food up from the kitchen.
sentences.n: The two women are brought under one roof, and neither knows who the other is.

sentences.t: Als der Tag heran kam, wo die Braut mit dem Bräutigam in die Kirche gehen sollte,
sentences.l: When the day came round on which the bride was to go to church with the bridegroom,
sentences.i: When the day came on which the bride was to go to church with the bridegroom,
sentences.n: “heran kommen” = to draw near, its particle split off. “wo” here stands for an dem, ‘on which’ — an everyday looseness of spoken German. Going to church is the wedding itself.

sentences.t: so schämte sie sich ihrer Häßlichkeit und fürchtete wenn sie sich auf der Straße zeigte, würde sie von den Leuten verspottet und ausgelacht.
sentences.l: she was ashamed of her ugliness and feared [that] if she showed herself in the street, she would be mocked and laughed at by the people.
sentences.i: she grew ashamed of her ugliness, and feared that if she showed herself in the street the people would mock her and laugh at her.
sentences.n: “sich schämen” takes the genitive: ihrer Häßlichkeit. The fear-clause has no daß to introduce it — the word order alone marks it as subordinate — so the literal supplies the bracketed ‘that’.

sentences.t: Da sprach sie zur Jungfrau Maleen „dir steht ein großes Glück bevor, ich habe mir den Fuß vertreten und kann nicht gut über die Straße gehen:
sentences.l: Then she said to Maiden Maleen “a great good fortune stands before you, I have twisted my foot and cannot walk well across the street:
sentences.i: Then she said to Maiden Maleen, “A great piece of good fortune is in store for you: I have twisted my foot and cannot walk across the street:
sentences.n: “bevorstehen” = to be in store for somebody, separable: steht … bevor. “sich den Fuß vertreten” is to twist or sprain one’s foot, and not the vertreten that means ‘to represent’. The dative “mir” is the dative of possession: the foot is her own.

sentences.t: du sollst meine Brautkleider anziehen und meine Stelle einnehmen: eine größere Ehre kann dir nicht zu Theil werden.“
sentences.l: you shall put on my bridal clothes and take my place: a greater honour cannot fall to your share.”
sentences.i: you shall put on my bridal dress and take my place: no greater honour could fall to you.”
sentences.n: “einnehmen” here is to take or occupy a place, not the ‘take medicine’ sense the same verb carries elsewhere. “zu Theil werden” (modern zuteil werden) is the old turn for falling to somebody’s share. The offer is a command with a compliment wrapped round it.

sentences.t: Die Jungfrau Maleen aber schlug es aus und sagte „ich verlange keine Ehre, die mir nicht gebührt.“
sentences.l: But Maiden Maleen refused it and said “I ask for no honour that is not due to me.”
sentences.i: But Maiden Maleen refused, and said, “I want no honour that is not my due.”
sentences.n: “ausschlagen” = to refuse, decline, separable: schlug es aus. “gebühren” takes the dative — mir gebührt, it is due to me.

sentences.t: Es war auch vergeblich daß sie ihr Gold anbot.
sentences.l: It was also in vain that she offered her gold.
sentences.i: It was in vain, too, that she offered her gold.
sentences.n: “ihr” here is the dative ‘to her’, not a possessive: the false bride offers Maleen gold to make her agree.

sentences.t: Endlich sprach sie zornig „wenn du mir nicht gehorchst, so kostet es dir dein Leben:
sentences.l: At last she said angrily “if you do not obey me, then it costs you your life:
sentences.i: At last she said angrily, “If you do not obey me, it will cost you your life:
sentences.n: “gehorchen” takes the dative: mir gehorchst. “es kostet dir dein Leben” carries an extra dative that modern German has dropped — it costs you, of you, your life.

sentences.t: ich brauche nur ein Wort zu sagen, so wird dir der Kopf vor die Füße gelegt.“
sentences.l: I need only say one word, and your head will be laid before your feet.”
sentences.i: I need only say a word, and your head will be laid at your feet.”
sentences.n: The threat is beheading, given in the flat formula the tales keep for it. “brauchen … zu” = need only do something. Another dative of possession: dir der Kopf, ‘the head to you’, meaning your head.

sentences.t: Da mußte sie gehorchen und die prächtigen Kleider der Braut sammt ihrem Schmuck anlegen.
sentences.l: Then she had to obey and put on the splendid clothes of the bride together with her jewellery.
sentences.i: Then she had to obey, and put on the bride’s splendid clothes together with her jewels.
sentences.n: “anlegen” here is to put on clothing, and not the ‘take aim with a gun’ sense the same verb has elsewhere. “sammt” = samt, together with, in the 1857 spelling.

sentences.t: Als sie in den königlichen Saal eintrat erstaunten alle über ihre große Schönheit
sentences.l: When she stepped into the royal hall all were astonished at her great beauty
sentences.i: When she entered the royal hall everyone was astonished at her great beauty
sentences.n: “eintreten” = to step in, enter. “erstaunen über” takes the accusative — astonished at.

sentences.t: und der König sagte zu seinem Sohn „das ist die Braut, die ich dir ausgewählt habe und die du zur Kirche führen sollst.“
sentences.l: and the king said to his son “that is the bride whom I have chosen for you and whom you shall lead to church.”
sentences.i: and the king said to his son, “That is the bride I have chosen for you, and whom you are to lead to church.”
sentences.n: “auswählen” = to pick out, choose. The father has never seen the woman he chose either — nobody in the house has.

sentences.t: Der Bräutigam erstaunte und dachte „sie gleicht meiner Jungfrau Maleen, und ich würde glauben sie wäre es selbst, aber die sitzt schon lange im Thurn gefangen oder ist todt.“
sentences.l: The bridegroom was astonished and thought “she resembles my Maiden Maleen, and I would believe she was she herself, but that one has long sat captive in the tower or is dead.”
sentences.i: The bridegroom was astonished, and thought, “She is the very likeness of my Maiden Maleen, and I would believe it was she herself — but that one has long been sitting captive in the tower, or is dead.”
sentences.n: “gleichen” takes the dative: sie gleicht meiner Jungfrau Maleen. The “die” heading the last clause is a demonstrative, ‘that one’, pointing back to the Maleen he means. “todt” = tot in the 1857 spelling. He is looking straight at her and reasoning himself out of it.

sentences.t: Er nahm sie an der Hand und führte sie zur Kirche.
sentences.l: He took her by the hand and led her to the church.
sentences.i: He took her by the hand and led her to church.
sentences.n: German takes somebody ‘at’ the hand — an der Hand — where English says ‘by’.

sentences.t: An dem Wege stand ein Brennesselbusch, da sprach sie
sentences.l: On the way stood a nettle bush, then she said
sentences.i: By the wayside stood a nettle bush, and she said
sentences.n: The nettle bush that fed her in her hunger stands at the roadside, and she speaks to it. The three sayings she speaks at the three thresholds are all in Low German, though the tale’s prose — and her own answers to the king’s son — stay High German.

sentences.t:
„Brennettelbusch,
Brennettelbusch so klene,
wat steist du hier allene?
ik hef de Tyt geweten
da hef ik dy ungesaden
ungebraden eten.“
sentences.l:
“nettle-bush,
nettle-bush so small,
what do you stand here alone for?
I have known the time
when I have eaten you unboiled,
unroasted.”
sentences.i:
“Nettle bush,
nettle bush so small,
why do you stand here alone?
I have known the time
when I ate you neither boiled
nor roasted.”
sentences.n: The prose of this tale is ordinary High German, but every song and every formula spoken aloud switches into Low German (Plattdeutsch), the old speech of the north — the shift is abrupt and deliberate, and the glossary gives the High German word for each dialect form. Here: “Brennettelbusch” = Brennnesselbusch, the same plant the prose has just called a Brennesselbusch; “klene” = klein; “wat” = was; “steist” = stehst; “allene” = allein; “hef” = habe; “de Tyt geweten” = die Zeit gewußt; “dy” = dich; “ungesaden ungebraden” = ungesotten, ungebraten. She is remembering her hunger, when she and her maid lived on raw nettles. The German rhymes klene with allene and geweten with eten; Lectorium’s English does not rhyme.

sentences.t: „Was sprichst du da?“ fragte der Königssohn. „Nichts,“ antwortete sie, „ich dachte nur an die Jungfrau Maleen.“
sentences.l: “What are you saying there?” asked the king’s son. “Nothing,” she answered, “I was only thinking of Maiden Maleen.”
sentences.i: “What is that you are saying?” asked the king’s son. “Nothing,” she answered; “I was only thinking of Maiden Maleen.”
sentences.n: “an jemanden denken” = to think of somebody, with an and the accusative. The question and the answer are kept in one unit here, as the printing runs them.

sentences.t: Er verwunderte sich daß sie von ihr wußte, schwieg aber still.
sentences.l: He wondered that she knew of her, but kept silent still.
sentences.i: He wondered that she knew of her, but held his peace.
sentences.n: “sich verwundern” = to be surprised. “still schweigen” doubles the idea: to be silent and say nothing.

sentences.t: Als sie an den Steg vor dem Kirchhof kamen, sprach sie
sentences.l: When they came to the plank crossing before the churchyard, she said
sentences.n: “Steg” is a narrow plank crossing, here the stile or footbridge at the churchyard wall. The song calls it Karkstegels; the prose later calls it Kirchensteg and then Kirchsteg.

sentences.t:
„Karkstegels, brik nich,
Bün de rechte Brut nich.“
sentences.l:
“churchyard-plank, do not break,
[I] am not the right bride.”
sentences.i:
“Churchyard stile, do not break —
I am not the true bride.”
sentences.n: “Karkstegels” = Kirchsteg, the plank or stile crossing into the churchyard; “brik” = brich, break (imperative); “bün” = bin; “Brut” = Braut, bride, and not the English word it resembles. The subject ‘I’ is simply left out, as the dialect freely does, and the literal supplies it in square brackets. The German rhymes nich with nich.

sentences.t: „Was sprichst du da?“ fragte der Königssohn? „Nichts,“ antwortete sie, „ich dachte nur an die Jungfrau Maleen.“
sentences.l: “What are you saying there?” asked the king’s son. “Nothing,” she answered, “I was only thinking of Maiden Maleen.”
sentences.i: “What is that you are saying?” asked the king’s son. “Nothing,” she answered; “I was only thinking of Maiden Maleen.”
sentences.n: The exchange is repeated word for word, and the English keeps the same wording so the reader can see that the German did not move. The question mark after “fragte der Königssohn” is the 1857 printing’s own; a full stop stands in the same place a few lines earlier.

sentences.t: „Kennst du die Jungfrau Maleen?“ „Nein,“ antwortete sie, „wie sollt ich sie kennen, ich habe nur von ihr gehört.“
sentences.l: “Do you know Maiden Maleen?” “No,” she answered, “how should I know her, I have only heard of her.”
sentences.i: “Do you know Maiden Maleen?” “No,” she answered; “how should I know her? I have only heard of her.”
sentences.n: “kennen” is to know a person, as against wissen, to know a fact. “sollt” is the older sollte. This is the one outright lie she tells about herself.

sentences.t: Als sie an die Kirchthüre kamen, sprach sie abermals
sentences.l: When they came to the church door, she said once more
sentences.i: When they came to the church door, she spoke once more
sentences.n: “abermals” = once again, an elevated word. Three thresholds, three formulas: the bush, the stile, the door.

sentences.t:
„Karkendär, brik nich,
bün de rechte Brut nich.“
sentences.l:
“church-door, do not break,
[I] am not the right bride.”
sentences.i:
“Church door, do not break —
I am not the true bride.”
sentences.n: The same formula with the church door in place of the stile: “Karkendär” = Kirchentür. She says it at each threshold she crosses under another woman’s name, and the English keeps the same wording each time.

sentences.t: „Was sprichst du da?“ fragte er.
sentences.l: “What are you saying there?” asked he.
sentences.i: “What is that you are saying?” he asked.
sentences.n: The third time he asks, and the third time she puts him off with the same name.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ antwortete sie, „ich habe nur an die Jungfrau Maleen gedacht.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” she answered, “I have only been thinking of Maiden Maleen.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” she answered, “I was only thinking of Maiden Maleen.”
sentences.n: The perfect “habe … gedacht” where the two earlier answers used the simple past dachte; spoken German prefers the perfect, and the tale drifts into it here.

sentences.t: Da zog er ein kostbares Geschmeide hervor, legte es ihr an den Hals und hakte die Kettenringe in einander.
sentences.l: Then he drew out a costly necklace, laid it round her neck and hooked the chain-rings into one another.
sentences.i: Then he drew out a costly necklace, put it round her neck and hooked the links together.
sentences.n: “Geschmeide” is a piece of jewellery, here a chain for the neck, and it becomes the proof of who the true bride is. “hervorziehen” and “einhaken” both split: zog … hervor, hakte … in einander. This “hakte” belongs to einhaken, to hook together, not to the loshaken, to unhook, that the same form is elsewhere.

sentences.t: Darauf traten sie in die Kirche und der Priester legte vor dem Altar ihre Hände in einander und vermählte sie.
sentences.l: Thereupon they stepped into the church and the priest laid their hands into one another before the altar and wedded them.
sentences.i: Thereupon they entered the church, and before the altar the priest laid their hands together and married them.
sentences.n: “vermählen” is the elevated word for marrying a couple. The marriage is real, and the tale will insist on that at the end: it is Maleen who is married in the church, under another woman’s clothes.

sentences.t: Er führte sie zurück, aber sie sprach auf dem ganzen Weg kein Wort.
sentences.l: He led her back, but she spoke not a word on the whole way.
sentences.i: He led her back, but she did not speak a word the whole way.
sentences.n: “zurückführen” splits: führte … zurück. The three formulas were everything she said, and she says nothing on the way home.

sentences.t: Als sie wieder in dem königlichen Schloß angelangt waren, eilte sie in die Kammer der Braut, legte die prächtigen Kleider und den Schmuck ab,
sentences.l: When they had arrived back in the royal castle, she hurried into the bride’s chamber, laid off the splendid clothes and the jewellery,
sentences.i: When they had come back to the royal castle, she hurried into the bride’s chamber and took off the splendid clothes and the jewels,
sentences.n: “ablegen” = to take off clothing, separable: legte … ab — the exact opposite of the anlegen she was forced into.

sentences.t: zog ihren grauen Kittel an und behielt nur das Geschmeide um den Hals, das sie von dem Bräutigam empfangen hatte.
sentences.l: put on her grey smock and kept only the necklace round her neck that she had received from the bridegroom.
sentences.i: put on her grey smock, and kept only the necklace round her neck that she had received from the bridegroom.
sentences.n: “anziehen” splits: zog … an. The necklace she keeps is the one thing the false bride will not be able to account for, and it decides the tale.

sentences.t: Als die Nacht heran kam und die Braut in das Zimmer des Königssohns sollte geführt werden, so ließ sie den Schleier über ihr Gesicht fallen, damit er den Betrug nicht merken sollte.
sentences.l: When the night drew on and the bride was to be led into the king’s son’s room, she let the veil fall over her face, so that he should not notice the deception.
sentences.i: When night came on and the bride was to be led into the king’s son’s room, she let the veil fall over her face so that he should not notice the deception.
sentences.n: “sollte geführt werden” stacks a passive inside a modal, and the whole stack waits at the end of the clause. “damit” introduces the purpose. From here the false bride has to answer for words she never spoke.

sentences.t: Sobald alle Leute fortgegangen waren, sprach er zu ihr „was hast du doch zu dem Brennesselbusch gesagt, der an dem Weg stand?“
sentences.l: As soon as all the people had gone away, he said to her “what was it you said to the nettle bush that stood by the way?”
sentences.i: As soon as everyone had gone, he said to her, “What was it you said to the nettle bush that stood by the road?”
sentences.n: The particle “doch” presses the question — ‘what was it, then’. He has been turning her three sayings over all day.

sentences.t: „Zu welchem Brennesselbusch?“ fragte sie, „ich spreche mit keinem Brennesselbusch.“ „Wenn du es nicht gethan hast, so bist du die rechte Braut nicht“ sagte er.
sentences.l: “To what nettle bush?” she asked, “I do not speak with any nettle bush.” “If you have not done it, then you are not the right bride,” he said.
sentences.i: “To what nettle bush?” she asked; “I do not talk to nettle bushes.” “If you did not do it, then you are not the true bride,” he said.
sentences.n: “gethan” = getan in the 1857 spelling. “die rechte Braut” — rechte here is ‘true, rightful’ — comes back four times in this tale, each time a shade more dangerous for her.

sentences.t: Da half sie sich und sprach
sentences.l: Then she helped herself and said
sentences.i: Then she found a way out, and said
sentences.n: “sich helfen” = to help oneself out of a fix. What follows is in Low German too: the false bride uses the same dialect the true bride used.

sentences.t:
„mut herut na myne Maegt,
de my myn Gedanken draegt.“
sentences.l:
“[it] must out to my maid,
who carries my thoughts for me.”
sentences.i:
“This must go out to my maid,
the one who carries my thoughts for me.”
sentences.n: The false bride’s own formula, and she uses it each time she is caught out: the answer must be fetched from the girl who did the speaking. “mut herut” = muß heraus, with no subject expressed, so the literal supplies ‘it’ in square brackets; “na” = nach, to; “Maegt” = Magd; “my”, “myn” = mir, mein; “draegt” = trägt. Maegt and draegt rhyme in the German.

sentences.t: Sie gieng hinaus und fuhr die Jungfrau Maleen an, „Dirne, was hast du zu dem Brennesselbusch gesagt?“
sentences.l: She went out and rounded on Maiden Maleen, “Girl, what did you say to the nettle bush?”
sentences.i: She went out and turned on Maiden Maleen: “Girl, what did you say to the nettle bush?”
sentences.n: “jemanden anfahren” = to snap at somebody, to round on them, separable: fuhr … an. “Dirne” in 1857 is simply a girl or a lass, without the pejorative sense the word took on later.

sentences.t: „Ich sagte nichts als
sentences.l: “I said nothing but
sentences.n: The sentence runs straight on into the song, and the quotation stays open across the verse.

sentences.t:
Brennettelbusch,
Brennettelbusch so klene,
wat steist du hier allene?
Ik hef de Tyt geweten,
da hef ik dy ungesaden
ungebraden eten.“
sentences.l:
Nettle-bush,
nettle-bush so small,
what do you stand here alone for?
I have known the time
when I have eaten you unboiled,
unroasted.”
sentences.i:
Nettle bush,
nettle bush so small,
why do you stand here alone?
I have known the time
when I ate you neither boiled
nor roasted.”
sentences.n: The same song word for word, now spoken by Maleen to the woman who will repeat it as her own — the English keeps the same wording so the reader can see that the German did not change. Only the capital of “Ik” and a comma differ from the first printing, and the opening quotation mark is missing because the quotation opened in the prose above.

sentences.t: Die Braut lief in die Kammer zurück und sagte „jetzt weiß ich was ich zu dem Brennesselbusch gesprochen habe,“ und wiederholte die Worte, die sie eben gehört hatte.
sentences.l: The bride ran back into the chamber and said “now I know what I said to the nettle bush,” and repeated the words that she had just heard.
sentences.i: The bride ran back into the chamber and said, “Now I know what I said to the nettle bush,” and repeated the words she had just heard.
sentences.n: “eben” here is ‘just now’. She has to be fed her own lines, one threshold at a time.

sentences.t: „Aber was sagtest du zu dem Kirchensteg, als wir darüber giengen?“ fragte der Königssohn.
sentences.l: “But what did you say to the church-plank when we went over it?” asked the king’s son.
sentences.i: “But what did you say to the church stile when we went over it?” asked the king’s son.
sentences.n: “sagtest” is the plain second-person past, du sagtest. “darüber” packs the preposition and its object into one word: over it.

sentences.t: „Zu dem Kirchensteg?“ antwortete sie, „ich spreche mit keinem Kirchensteg.“ „Dann bist du auch die rechte Braut nicht.“
sentences.l: “To the church-plank?” she answered, “I do not speak with any church-plank.” “Then you are not the right bride either.”
sentences.i: “To the church stile?” she answered; “I do not talk to church stiles.” “Then you are not the true bride either.”
sentences.n: The same exchange as before with one word changed; the repetition is the tale’s engine. “auch … nicht” = not … either.

sentences.t: Sie sagte wiederum
sentences.l: She said once again
sentences.n: “wiederum” = once again.

sentences.t:
„mut herut na myne Maegt,
de my myn Gedanken draegt.“
sentences.l:
“[it] must out to my maid,
who carries my thoughts for me.”
sentences.i:
“This must go out to my maid,
the one who carries my thoughts for me.”
sentences.n: The same formula, unchanged, and it will come once more.

sentences.t: Lief hinaus und fuhr die Jungfrau Maleen an, „Dirne, was hast du zu dem Kirchsteg gesagt?“
sentences.l: Ran out and rounded on Maiden Maleen, “Girl, what did you say to the church-plank?”
sentences.i: [She] ran out and turned on Maiden Maleen: “Girl, what did you say to the church stile?”
sentences.n: The subject is missing at the head of the sentence: the printing simply starts with the verb and carries “sie” over from before. The literal leaves the gap open and the idiomatic supplies the pronoun in square brackets. The word is Kirchsteg here and Kirchensteg a moment ago; the printing uses both forms.

sentences.t: „Ich sagte nichts als
sentences.l: “I said nothing but
sentences.n: Again the quotation runs open into the song.

sentences.t:
Karkstegels, brik nich,
bün de rechte Brut nich.“
sentences.l:
Churchyard-plank, do not break,
[I] am not the right bride.”
sentences.i:
Churchyard stile, do not break —
I am not the true bride.”
sentences.n: The stile formula again, word for word; only its opening quotation mark is gone, because the quotation opened in the prose above.

sentences.t: „Das kostet dich dein Leben“ rief die Braut, eilte aber in die Kammer und sagte „jetzt weiß ich was ich zu dem Kirchsteg gesprochen habe“ und wiederholte die Worte.
sentences.l: “That costs you your life,” cried the bride, but hurried into the chamber and said “now I know what I said to the church-plank,” and repeated the words.
sentences.i: “That will cost you your life,” cried the bride — but she hurried into the chamber and said, “Now I know what I said to the church stile,” and repeated the words.
sentences.n: The threat and the errand in one breath: she must have the words even as she promises to kill the girl for them. Here the accusative “dich” where the earlier threat had the dative “dir”.

sentences.t: „Aber was sagtest du zur Kirchenthür?“
sentences.l: “But what did you say to the church door?”
sentences.n: “zur” = zu der. The printing has Kirchenthür here, Kirchenthüre a few lines on and Kirchthüre earlier; all three are left as they stand.

sentences.t: „Zur Kirchenthür?“ antwortete sie, „ich spreche mit keiner Kirchenthür.“ „Dann bist du auch die rechte Braut nicht.“
sentences.l: “To the church door?” she answered, “I do not speak with any church door.” “Then you are not the right bride either.”
sentences.i: “To the church door?” she answered; “I do not talk to church doors.” “Then you are not the true bride either.”
sentences.n: The third and last of the three thresholds.

sentences.t: Sie gieng hinaus, fuhr die Jungfrau Maleen an „Dirne, was hast du zu der Kirchenthür gesagt?“
sentences.l: She went out, rounded on Maiden Maleen “Girl, what did you say to the church door?”
sentences.i: She went out and turned on Maiden Maleen: “Girl, what did you say to the church door?”
sentences.n: The two verbs stand side by side with only a comma and no und — the printing hurries here.

sentences.t: „Ich sagte nichts als
sentences.l: “I said nothing but
sentences.n: The same opening for the third time.

sentences.t:
Karkendär, brik nich,
bün de rechte Brut nich.“
sentences.l:
Church-door, do not break,
[I] am not the right bride.”
sentences.i:
Church door, do not break —
I am not the true bride.”
sentences.n: The last of the three formulas, and the last of the songs until the children’s rhyme at the end.

sentences.t: „Das bricht dir den Hals“ rief die Braut und gerieth in den größten Zorn, eilte aber zurück in die Kammer und sagte „jetzt weiß ich was ich zu der Kirchenthür gesprochen habe,“ und wiederholte die Worte.
sentences.l: “That breaks your neck,” cried the bride and fell into the greatest rage, but hurried back into the chamber and said “now I know what I said to the church door,” and repeated the words.
sentences.i: “That will break your neck,” cried the bride, and flew into the greatest rage — but she hurried back into the chamber and said, “Now I know what I said to the church door,” and repeated the words.
sentences.n: The dative of possession again: dir den Hals, ‘the neck to you’, meaning your neck. Her threats climb — your life, your neck — and she still has to run the errand.

sentences.t: „Aber, wo hast du das Geschmeide, das ich dir an der Kirchenthüre gab?“ „Was für ein Geschmeide,“ antwortete sie, „du hast mir kein Geschmeide gegeben.“
sentences.l: “But where do you have the necklace that I gave you at the church door?” “What kind of a necklace,” she answered, “you have given me no necklace.”
sentences.i: “But where is the necklace I gave you at the church door?” “What necklace?” she answered. “You gave me no necklace.”
sentences.n: German asks ‘where do you have it’ where English asks ‘where is it’. The comma after “Aber” is the printing’s own. This is the one question the girl in the kitchen cannot answer for her.

sentences.t: „Ich habe es dir selbst um den Hals gelegt und selbst eingehakt: wenn du das nicht weißt, so bist du die rechte Braut nicht.“
sentences.l: “I laid it round your neck myself and hooked it myself: if you do not know that, then you are not the right bride.”
sentences.i: “I put it round your neck with my own hands and hooked it myself: if you do not know that, then you are not the true bride.”
sentences.n: “selbst” twice, both times ‘myself’. “weißt” is wissen, to know a fact, as against the kennen, to know a person, of the earlier exchange.

sentences.t: Er zog ihr den Schleier vom Gesicht,
sentences.l: He drew the veil from her face,
sentences.i: He pulled the veil from her face,
sentences.n: Once more the dative of possession — ihr den Schleier, ‘the veil from her’ — where English uses a possessive.

sentences.t: und als er ihre grundlose Häßlichkeit erblickte, sprang er erschrocken zurück und sprach „wie kommst du hierher? wer bist du?“
sentences.l: and when he caught sight of her fathomless ugliness, he sprang back startled and said “how do you come here? who are you?”
sentences.i: and when he saw her fathomless ugliness, he sprang back in horror and said, “How do you come to be here? Who are you?”
sentences.n: “grundlos” is literally ‘bottomless’ — an ugliness with no floor to it. The small w of “wer” after the question mark is the printing’s own.

sentences.t: „Ich bin deine verlobte Braut, aber weil ich fürchtete die Leute würden mich verspotten, wenn sie mich draußen erblickten,
sentences.l: “I am your betrothed bride, but because I feared the people would mock me if they caught sight of me outside,
sentences.i: “I am your betrothed bride; but because I feared the people would mock me if they saw me out of doors,
sentences.n: The fear-clause again runs on without daß. “würden … verspotten” and “erblickten” are the subjunctive of reported thought.

sentences.t: so habe ich dem Aschenputtel befohlen meine Kleider anzuziehen und statt meiner zur Kirche zu gehen.“
sentences.l: so I have ordered the ash-girl to put on my clothes and to go to church instead of me.”
sentences.i: so I ordered the kitchen girl to put on my clothes and go to church in my place.”
sentences.n: “befehlen” takes the dative of the person: dem Aschenputtel. “statt meiner” is the genitive of the pronoun after statt, an old construction. “anzuziehen” sets the zu inside the separable verb: an-zu-ziehen.

sentences.t: „Wo ist das Mädchen“ sagte er, „ich will es sehen, geh und hol es hierher.“
sentences.l: “Where is the girl,” said he, “I want to see it, go and fetch it here.”
sentences.i: “Where is the girl?” said he. “I want to see her — go and fetch her here.”
sentences.n: German calls a girl das Mädchen, a neuter noun, so its pronoun is “es”, ‘it’; the literal keeps that and the idiomatic says ‘her’. The printing gives no question mark after Mädchen.

sentences.t: Sie gieng hinaus und sagte den Dienern das Aschenputtel sei eine Betrügerin, sie sollten es in den Hof hinabführen und ihm den Kopf abschlagen.
sentences.l: She went out and told the servants the ash-girl was a cheat, they should lead it down into the courtyard and strike off its head.
sentences.i: She went out and told the servants that the kitchen girl was an impostor, and that they should take her down into the courtyard and strike off her head.
sentences.n: “sei” and “sollten” are the subjunctive of reported speech, and they are what tells the reader these are her words and not the tale’s. “Hof” here is the courtyard, not the court. The order is given as flatly as everything else in this tale.

sentences.t: Die Diener packten es und wollten es fortschleppen, aber es schrie so laut um Hilfe, daß der Königssohn seine Stimme vernahm, aus seinem Zimmer herbei eilte und den Befehl gab das Mädchen augenblicklich loszulassen.
sentences.l: The servants seized it and wanted to drag it away, but it cried so loud for help that the king’s son heard its voice, hurried up out of his room and gave the order to let the girl go at once.
sentences.i: The servants seized her and were about to drag her off, but she cried so loud for help that the king’s son heard her voice, came hurrying from his room and gave the order to let the girl go at once.
sentences.n: “seine Stimme” — the possessive follows the grammatical gender of Mädchen, so the German says ‘his voice’ of a girl, which English cannot do; the literal quietly says ‘its’. “herbei eilen” = to come hurrying up; “loszulassen” sets its zu inside the verb: los-zu-lassen.

sentences.t: Es wurden Lichter herbei geholt und da bemerkte er an ihrem Hals den Goldschmuck den er ihm vor der Kirchenthür gegeben hatte.
sentences.l: Lights were fetched, and then he noticed on her neck the gold ornament that he had given it before the church door.
sentences.i: Lights were brought, and then he saw at her neck the gold necklace he had given her before the church door.
sentences.n: The gender wavers inside a single sentence: “ihrem Hals” treats her as a woman, “ihm … gegeben” treats her as das Mädchen. The 1857 text does both and is left as it stands. “Es wurden Lichter geholt” opens with a placeholder es that carries no meaning of its own.

sentences.t: „Du bist die rechte Braut“ sagte er, „die mit mir zur Kirche gegangen ist: komm mit mir in meine Kammer.“
sentences.l: “You are the right bride,” said he, “who went to church with me: come with me into my chamber.”
sentences.i: “You are the true bride,” said he, “the one who went to church with me: come with me into my chamber.”
sentences.n: The relative clause is cut loose from its noun by the speech tag and picks up again after it. “die rechte Braut” for the last time, and now it is said to the right woman.

sentences.t: Als sie beide allein waren, sprach er „du hast auf dem Kirchgang die Jungfrau Maleen genannt, die meine verlobte Braut war:
sentences.l: When they were both alone, he said “on the way to church you named Maiden Maleen, who was my betrothed bride:
sentences.i: When the two of them were alone, he said, “On the way to church you named Maiden Maleen, who was my betrothed bride:
sentences.n: “Kirchgang” is the going to church, here the wedding procession itself. “nennen” = to name, to mention.

sentences.t: wenn ich dächte es wäre möglich, so müßte ich glauben sie stände vor mir: du gleichst ihr in allem.“
sentences.l: if I thought it were possible, I should have to believe she stood before me: you resemble her in everything.”
sentences.i: if I thought it possible, I should have to believe she was standing before me: you are like her in everything.”
sentences.n: Four subjunctives in a row — dächte, wäre, müßte, stände — the mood of the unreal, and the whole sentence hangs on them. “gleichen” again with the dative: du gleichst ihr.

sentences.t: Sie antwortete „ich bin die Jungfrau Maleen, die um dich sieben Jahre in der Finsterniß gefangen gesessen, Hunger und Durst gelitten und so lange in Noth und Armuth gelebt hat:
sentences.l: She answered “I am Maiden Maleen, who for your sake sat captive seven years in the darkness, suffered hunger and thirst and lived so long in need and poverty:
sentences.i: She answered, “I am Maiden Maleen, who for your sake sat captive seven years in the darkness, suffered hunger and thirst, and lived so long in want and poverty:
sentences.n: “um dich” = for your sake. Three past participles hang on the single “hat” at the end — gesessen, gelitten, gelebt — a chain German holds open and English has to break up. “Finsterniß”, “Noth” and “Armuth” are all 1857 spellings of Finsternis, Not and Armut.

sentences.t: aber heute bescheint mich die Sonne wieder.
sentences.l: but today the sun shines on me again.
sentences.i: but today the sun shines upon me again.
sentences.n: “bescheinen” = to shine upon, and it takes the person as its object, which English cannot quite do. After seven years walled away from sun and moon, this is the whole of her complaint and the whole of her joy.

sentences.t: Ich bin dir in der Kirche angetraut und bin deine rechtmäßige Gemahlin.“
sentences.l: I am wedded to you in the church and am your lawful wife.”
sentences.i: I was wedded to you in the church, and I am your lawful wife.”
sentences.n: “antrauen” = to wed one person to another, with the dative: dir angetraut. Her claim is legal as much as sentimental — the marriage in the church was performed on her.

sentences.t: Da küßten sie einander und waren glücklich für ihr Lebtag.
sentences.l: Then they kissed one another and were happy for their lifetime.
sentences.i: Then they kissed one another and were happy all their days.
sentences.n: “für ihr Lebtag” is an old fixed phrase, ‘for their life-day’, meaning all their lives.

sentences.t: Der falschen Braut ward zur Vergeltung der Kopf abgeschlagen.
sentences.l: The false bride’s head was struck off in requital.
sentences.i: As requital, the false bride’s head was struck off.
sentences.n: The dative of possession one last time: der falschen Braut … der Kopf. “zur Vergeltung” = in requital, in payment. The tale offers this as justice, in one sentence, and says nothing more; it is the same beheading she twice threatened, turned around.

sentences.t: Der Thurn, in welchem die Jungfrau Maleen gesessen hatte, stand noch lange Zeit,
sentences.l: The tower in which Maiden Maleen had sat stood for a long time yet,
sentences.i: The tower in which Maiden Maleen had sat stood for a long time afterwards,
sentences.n: “in welchem” is the more formal relative, where the tale elsewhere says in dem. The story is over and the tower is still standing — a coda that pushes the tale out into the world the children live in.

sentences.t: und wenn die Kinder vorüber giengen, so sangen sie
sentences.l: and when the children went past, they sang
sentences.i: and whenever the children went past, they sang
sentences.n: “vorübergehen” splits: giengen … vorüber, in the 1857 spelling. What follows is the last of the Low German, and it is not the story’s own voice but a children’s street rhyme.

sentences.t:
„kling klang kloria,
wer sitt in dissen Thoria?
Dar sitt en Königsdochter in,
die kann ik nich to seen krygn.
De Muer de will nich bräken,
de Steen de will nich stechen.
Hänschen mit de bunte Jak,
kumm unn folg my achterna.“
sentences.l:
“kling klang kloria,
who sits in this tower?
There sits a king’s-daughter in it,
whom I cannot get to see.
The wall it will not break,
the stone it will not give way.
Little-Hans with the bright-coloured jacket,
come and follow after me.”
sentences.i:
“Kling, klang, kloria,
who sits inside this tower?
A king’s daughter sits within,
and I cannot get sight of her.
The wall will not break,
the stone will not give way.
Little Hans in the gay-coloured jacket,
come along and follow after me.”
sentences.n: The children’s rhyme that outlives the story, sung at the tower long after. “kling klang kloria” is a chiming nonsense refrain, and “klang” here belongs to it and is not the past tense of klingen; “Thoria” is Turm bent into a rhyme for it. “sitt” = sitzt; “dissen” = diesem; “Königsdochter” = Königstochter; “to seen krygn” = zu sehen kriegen, to get sight of; “Muer” = Mauer; “bräken” = brechen; “Steen” = Stein; “unn” = und; “achterna” = hinterher. What “de Steen de will nich stechen” means exactly is arguable: stechen answers bräken as a rhyme-word, and the sense is something like the stone refusing to shift or be prised out — the line is not certain, and this rendering does not pretend it is. “Hänschen mit de bunte Jak” arrives from nowhere, as the tag-ends of children’s songs do.

glossary.anlegen: anlegen — to put on (clothes, jewellery); separable: legt an
glossary.drang: dringen — penetrated, made its way (3rd sg. past; durch etwas dringen, to get through something)
glossary.einnehmen: einnehmen — to take, to occupy (a place); separable, particle ein (meine Stelle einnehmen, to take my place)
glossary.fuhr: anfahren — rounded on, snapped at (3rd sg. past; separable an-: fuhr … an); the plain fahren means to go, to travel
glossary.gebrochen: brechen — broken (past participle; ob dein trotziger Sinn gebrochen ist, whether your defiant spirit is broken)
glossary.gerade: gerade — just, exactly, precisely (gerade der Verlobte, precisely the betrothed)
glossary.glauben: glauben — to believe (ich würde glauben, I would believe); also der Glauben, belief
glossary.hakte: einhaken — hooked together, fastened (3rd sg. past; separable ein-: hakte … in einander)
glossary.hieß: heißen — bade, told (3rd sg. past; jemanden etwas thun heißen, to bid somebody do something: hieß man sie weiter gehen); also was called (die hieß Jungfrau Maleen)
glossary.klang: klang — the second chiming syllable of the children’s rhyme (kling klang kloria), not the past of klingen
glossary.laut: laut — loud, aloud (adv.); also der Laut, a sound (kein Laut drang durch die Mauern)
glossary.schloß: schließen — shut, closed (3rd sg. past; sich einschließen, to shut oneself in: schloß sich … ein); also das Schloß — castle (1857 spelling of Schloss)
glossary.sei: sein — is, be (3rd sg. present subjunctive of reported speech: sie sagte, das Aschenputtel sei eine Betrügerin); also the imperative sei, be!
glossary.spreche: sprechen — speak, talk (1st sg. present: ich spreche mit keinem …, I do not talk to any …)
glossary.stechen: Low German (Plattdeutsch): stechen — (of a stone) to shift, to be prised out; the exact sense in ‘de Steen de will nich stechen’ is arguable, the word answering bräken as a rhyme
glossary.trank: der Trank — drink, draught (Speise und Trank = food and drink); also trinken — drank (3rd sg. past)
glossary.verlobte: verloben — to betroth (past participle used as adjective and as noun: die verlobte Braut, der Verlobte; the same spelling can also be the 3rd sg. past)
glossary.vertreten: vertreten — to twist, to sprain (sich den Fuß vertreten, to twist one’s foot)
glossary.wann: wann — when (the question word: wußten nicht wann Tag oder Nacht anbrach, did not know when day or night broke)
